newsitem.title: UK: UK fund managers positive on gilts - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK fund managers positive on gilts - survey.

text.p: UK fund managers swung to their most positive stance on gilts for two-and-a-half years, and their most negative stance on domestic equities in a year, in the wake of the budget on July 2, a survey showed on Monday.

The poll of 56 institutions controlling funds totalling 775 billion stg found that interest rate expectations had deteriorated in the wake of the budget, undercutting prospects for growth in the economy and in company profits.
Equally, the budget's abolition of tax relief for pension funds on share dividends increased the appeal of gilts relative to equities, the poll said.

The monthly survey, carried out by pollsters Gallup for investment bank Merrill Lynch, found that buyers of gilts outnumbered sellers by 29 percent, the highest rating for UK government bonds since December 1994.
Yet for UK equities, sellers outnumbered buyers by 18 percent, the most negative reading since last July.
"The UK equity market is contending with the prospect of higher base rates," said Merrill global strategist Bijal Shah.
"In contrast, interest rates are not rising on the continent. As a result, we believe UK equities will perform poorly when compared with other European bourses."

After a budget which did less than some expected to raise taxes on buoyant UK consumers to dampen inflationary pressures, the Merrill survey found that fund managers were more pessimistic on the outlook for interest rates.
The UK's base lending rate was seen at 7.5 percent in 12 months' time, compared with 7.1 percent in last months' poll.

At the same time, sentiment towards sterling saw a sharp upturn on the back of rising rates, with 33 percent seeing it as their favourite currency for the next 12 months compared with 13 percent in the previous poll. The dollar remained top currency, favoured by 43 percent -- down from 57 percent.

Sterling strength has already been a significant negative for a swathe of UK firms, one reason for the underperformance of some international stocks and exporters such as British Steel Plc and Imperial Chemical Industries Plc.
The Merrill poll found that the engineering sector remained as the least favourite group, with a negative balance of 11.2 percent.

Food retailers, which saw a major recovery last week, were voted most favourite with a positive balance of 9.2 percent -- another reflection of expectations that consumer spending will remain robust in the wake of the budget.

"The domestic economy is growing at a healthy pace," said Shah. "Consumer spending should remain strong given the windfall gains to consumers from the restructuring of the UK building societies and mutual insurance companies."
"In our view, consumer spending can only be curtailed by a significant rise in base rates, perhaps to eight percent."
A net 34 percent expected the UK equity market to be lower in three months' time, with expected earnings per share growth shaved to 7.7 percent in 1997 from 8.5 percent in June.
For 1998, eps was seen growing 6.8 percent, down from 7.8 percent.
Ironically given the perception of upward pressure on inflation, inflation expectations were nudged down to 2.9 percent from 3.0 percent in the previous poll.
Full results of the poll, taken between July 7 and 9, were as follows:
Asset class July vote (pct) June vote (pct)
UK equities -18 -12
UK bonds +29 +17
U.S. equities -11 -4
Cont. Euro. equities -2 -7
Japanese equities +32 +26
Pacific basin equities +2 +1
Cash -18 -24
Bonds outside UK +5 -1
UK index-linked gilts +13 +7
UK property +13 +19
